name: ADP
headline: The payroll company one in six US workers depends on, with clients who rarely leave.
what_short: Payroll, tax and HR services for employers
what_it_does: ADP runs payroll, payroll tax filing, HR, benefits and time tracking for over 1.1 million employer clients, paying more than 42 million workers. It also acts as a co-employer for about 762,000 worksite employees. It earns extra interest on the client money it holds between paying in and paying out.
why_it_passed: Payroll and tax filing are tasks every employer must do correctly, so clients stay: it keeps 92.1% of its client revenue each year, up from 89.9% ten years ago.
Moving to another provider takes six to nine months and a payroll mistake is costly, so clients rarely switch on price alone.
It is connected directly to tens of thousands of government agencies, tax authorities and banks, a network rivals find hard to copy.
It needs very little added capital to grow: about 65% a year after tax on the capital it uses, counting past purchases.
why_not_now: The analysis puts the value at $156 to $246 a share, and the price was $260.26, above the top of that range. At that price a buyer would expect roughly 5.4% to 7.4% a year, about level with a 30-year US Treasury bond (5.66%), which carries far less risk.
watch: About a quarter of pre-tax earnings comes from interest on client funds, so falling interest rates would cut profit.
Younger rivals (Paycom, Paylocity) are growing faster, and AI or cheap payroll software could make the service more of a commodity.
It has bought back shares at prices above the bottom of the value range, and it borrows short-term to support the client funds.
